title: Zero-Carbon Hydrogen Burner for Domestic Heating
context: FEEG6013 Group Design Project, University of Southampton
role: Team of five. I led the team through the design lifecycle and led the CFD model.
summary: A perforated plate burner that runs on methane and hydrogen: designed, built and fire-tested, with a CFD model that diagnosed a flame problem in the lab and predicted hydrogen performance.

facts.label: hydrogen combustion predicted at equivalence ratio 0.4, no flashback
CFD pressure drop against theory (56.95 Pa vs 59.82 Pa)
polyhedral cells at mesh independence

sections.heading: The brief
body: Domestic heating, mostly from natural gas boilers, accounted for 18% of UK greenhouse gas emissions in 2021. The brief was a perforated plate burner able to run on both methane and hydrogen, delivering 10 kW with a 5:1 turn-down ratio to match existing domestic boilers.

figures.caption: Exploded view of the final design: inlet pipe, plenum, perforated plate and ignition mount

sections.heading: Design and build
body: I led the team from concept generation and design requirements through prototyping, testing and validation. I evaluated manufacturing processes and joining methods against operating conditions and failure modes, and used CNC machining to make prototype components.

figures.caption: Assembled burner with ignition system on the test rig
Blowout stability map from the team's tests: stable region shaded, design point marked

sections.heading: The CFD model
body: I built the model in ANSYS Fluent with RANS k-omega SST turbulence and GRI-Mech 3.0 finite-rate chemistry. The mesh used polyhedral cells with wall-resolved inflation layers and local refinement, and reached mesh independence at 2.3 million cells. A periodic radial slice kept the computational cost down. Teammates adopted the workflow for their own simulations.
As a first check, the predicted pressure drop across the plate (56.95 Pa) came within 4.8% of the theoretical value (59.82 Pa).

figures.caption: Polyhedral mesh of the burner's internal volume, with local refinement and inflation layers

sections.heading: Checking it against the experiment
body: Cold-flow velocities through the plate followed the measured radial trend, including the dip at the centre, but over-predicted absolute values by 34.4% on average. RANS time-averaging of the unstable jet shear layers and pitot probe placement explain most of that gap, so the model was used for trends and flame behaviour rather than absolute velocity.

figures.caption: Radial velocity through the plate: experiment (solid) against CFD (dashed) across eight flow rates

sections.heading: Diagnosing the missing flames
body: In the reactive tests the outer three rings of holes would not light. The methane model reproduced this: OH and temperature fields showed ambient air diluting the mixture at the edge of the plate. That finding led to a quartz shroud, which gave a uniform flame across every hole.

figures.caption: Methane: temperature above the plate, cooler over the outer holes
OH mass fraction 1 mm above the plate; low OH marks the unlit outer rings
With the shroud fitted: flame across every hole at 10 kW

sections.heading: Extending it to hydrogen
body: Hydrogen could not be tested in the lab, so the validated model was extended to it, with a 9-species mechanism and preferential diffusion enabled, and the inlet Reynolds number matched to the 10 kW methane case.

It predicted stable combustion at 8.2 kW and equivalence ratio 0.4 with no flashback. Predicted flames were about 2.4 mm tall against 3.6 mm for methane, consistent with hydrogen's much higher flame speed.

figures.caption: Hydrogen: predicted temperature field above the plate

evidence: The group design report can be shared on request. Photos and test data are team outputs; the CFD model is my lead work.

title: NACA 0012 Airfoil RANS CFD Analysis
context: FEEG6005 Applications of CFD, University of Southampton
summary: A 2D steady RANS study from -11 to +15 degrees angle of attack, matched to NASA data on lift, with a clear account of why drag disagreed.

facts.label: lift coefficient error against NASA experiment
lift change between meshes, while drag moved 25%
estimated near-stall angle of attack

sections.heading: What I did
body: I ran a 2D steady RANS analysis of a NACA 0012 airfoil from -11 to +15 degrees angle of attack in ANSYS Fluent, producing lift and drag polars and a near-stall estimate of about 14.5 degrees.

sections.heading: Choosing the turbulence model
body: I chose the turbulence model from a y+ estimate rather than by default. The first cells sat in the buffer layer, so I used RNG k-epsilon with wall functions on the coarse mesh. After refining the mesh with Fluent's Adapt function to reach y+ of about 2.9, I switched to Spalart-Allmaras.

figures.caption: Adapted mesh near the leading edge

sections.heading: Convergence
body: Lift converged to within 0.2% between meshes, while drag changed by about 25%. That showed drag was the near-wall-sensitive quantity and that the refined mesh gave the figure to trust.

sections.heading: Comparison with experiment
body: Lift matched NASA experimental data to within 1.6%. I explained the larger drag gap with three causes: a Reynolds number roughly 7 times lower than the dataset, wall-function error, and the model treating the boundary layer as turbulent from the leading edge.
Reynolds-similarity scaling, with geometry and fluid properties scaled together, preserved the coefficients to within 0.6%.

figures.caption: Pressure coefficient: CFD against experimental data

sections.heading: Next
body: Repeat the study in SU2 or OpenFOAM and compare the open-source results with Fluent. This is the first project on my simulation learning track.

takeaway: Converged residuals do not mean a correct answer. Separating numerical error from modelling error, and reporting confidence per quantity, is what makes a CFD result usable.
evidence: The project report and Fluent setup can be shared on request.

title: Mechatronic Pitch Mechanism for a Wind Tunnel
context: FEEG3003 Individual Project, University of Southampton
role: Individual project: mechanism design, electronics, control code, FEA, build and wind tunnel testing.
summary: A low-cost rig that sets a model's angle of attack inside the wind tunnel, using two linear actuators under PI control with IMU feedback. Designed, analysed, built and tested on a £110 budget.

facts.label: total build cost against a £110 budget
margin on natural frequency, against a requirement of 2
blockage ratio, under the 5% limit

hero.caption: Installed in the wind tunnel, holding a cylinder at 30° angle of attack

sections.heading: The brief
body: Experimental aerodynamics research at Southampton needed a stable, repeatable way to change a model's angle of attack. The target was angles up to 30° at different vertical positions in the test section, within a £110 budget.

figures.caption: Early concept sketch

sections.heading: Mechanism design
body: Two linear actuators extend by different amounts to tilt a plate carrying the model. I mapped the maximum angle against actuator extension and spacing to choose the geometry, then checked the sensor's ±1.5° accuracy against that spacing with a relative error analysis.

figures.caption: Maximum angle of attack against half actuator extension and actuator spacing

sections.heading: Electronics and control
body: An Arduino UNO drives the actuators through an L298N motor driver, reads the angle from an MPU6050 IMU and drag from a load cell with an HX711 amplifier, and shows the angle on an I2C LCD.

A PI controller closes the loop on the IMU reading. I raised the integral gain until instability appeared, settling at 0.003. Measured step responses to 10° and 30° showed clear PI behaviour with a time constant of about 4 seconds; the actuators' constant extension speed is what limits it.

figures.caption: Control box: Arduino, motor driver and load cell amplifier
Step response to 30°: measured against a first-order analytical model

sections.heading: Structural and modal analysis
body: FEA in ANSYS under the modelled drag load put the peak stress at the rod base, as cantilever beam theory predicts, and a mesh convergence study settled at around 300,000 nodes.
The first six natural frequencies, from 53 Hz to 225 Hz, sit well clear of the wind tunnel's excitation range: a margin of 5.3 against a design requirement of 2.

figures.caption: Equivalent stress under the drag load
First mode shape, 53.24 Hz

sections.heading: Build
body: Mounts and actuator sleeves were 3D printed in PLA at 60% infill, with 6 mm plywood support plates fixed to the tunnel's top panel with T-nuts. The total came to £100.20.

figures.caption: Actuators assembled on the upper plate

sections.heading: Wind tunnel testing
body: I ran 15 datasets on a cylinder at 0° to 30° and 15 to 25 m/s, with tare runs and a load cell calibration before each run. The assembly's blockage ratio was 1.74%, well under the 5% limit.
Drag coefficient rose with angle of attack as flow separation moved forward. I compared the trend with published experimental and LES data and explained the differences through cylinder aspect ratio.

sections.heading: Next iteration
body: The IMU's ±1.5° accuracy is the limit for research use. On a similar budget a better IMU is the cheapest improvement; with more budget, feedback actuators would allow a double closed loop.

evidence: The individual project report (10,400 words) can be shared on request.

title: CPU Heat Sink Design and Fin Optimisation
context: SESM3032 Heat Transfer coursework, University of Southampton
summary: Fin optimisation in COMSOL, then a copper pin-fin heat sink for a 60 W CPU, iterated until it held 70°C, with a transient study and a throttling strategy for an overclocked load.

facts.label: peak CPU temperature at 60 W, under the 343 K (70°C) limit
maximum steady load the final design holds below 70°C
overclocked load run in 30 s bursts, alternating with half load to recover

hero.caption: Temperature field in the quarter-symmetry heat sink model

sections.heading: Starting with a single fin
body: I modelled a tapered radial fin in 2D axisymmetry and compared its temperature profile with the analytical plate fin solution. The two differ because the tapered fin’s cross-section changes along its length, which the plate fin equation does not capture.

Iterating length and thickness, then switching from aluminium to copper, raised fin effectiveness from 8.2 to 47.7 while keeping efficiency near 98%. A parametric sweep over thickness then found the shape for maximum heat transfer.

figures.caption: Tapered radial fin: 3D temperature distribution
Array of optimised fins on a tube condensing saturated steam

sections.heading: Fin array on a steam tube
body: An array of the optimised fins on a tube condensing saturated steam transferred 4.26 kW for an 80 mm tube, rising to 4.40 kW at 160 mm, with condensation rates from 1.88 to 1.95 g/s.

sections.heading: Sizing the CPU heat sink
body: For the CPU, a Newton’s law of cooling estimate showed the heat transfer coefficient a bare chip would need, which made the case for a heat spreader with fins.

A parametric sweep on a copper square pin fin with a fixed 120 mm³ volume gave an optimum of 1.9 mm by 31 mm, carrying 0.75 W each. That pointed to about 80 fins for a 60 W load, on a 30 mm radius spreader.

figures.caption: Heat transfer per pin fin against fin thickness, at fixed volume
Pin-fin array on a round heat spreader

sections.heading: Iterating to the limit
body: I cut the model to a quarter using symmetry, which brought solve times down to about 15 seconds, and put a probe at the hottest point above the CPU die. A sweep on spreader thickness set it at 5 mm, balancing temperature against material.

The first design reached 359 K at 60 W, well over the 343 K limit. More fins helped with diminishing returns (112 fins gave 350.45 K, 164 gave 347.14 K), so instead I raised the heat transfer coefficient to 100 W/m²K to reflect fan cooling. With 112 fins that gave 342 K, and the design holds the limit up to 62.47 W.

figures.caption: Quarter model mesh, using symmetry to cut solve time
Peak temperature against CPU load for the final design

sections.heading: Transient behaviour and throttling
body: A 200-second transient study at 60 W, 62.47 W and 65 W showed a time constant of about 140 seconds before the sink settles.

For an overclocked CPU, I modelled a periodic load: 75 W (1.2 times the maximum) for 30 seconds, the time it takes to approach the limit, then half load to recover. Peak temperature stays within 343 K, so the CPU can run overclocked for as long as possible without overheating.

figures.caption: Transient warm-up at 60 W
Dynamic load: peak temperature under the throttling cycle

evidence: The coursework report can be shared on request.

title: Wind Turbine Blade Finite Element Analysis
context: FEEG3001 Finite Element Analysis coursework, University of Southampton
summary: A structural model of a steel wind turbine blade under three load cases and a modal analysis, checked against beam theory, tested for mesh convergence, then used to judge the blade at its 20 m/s design wind speed.

facts.label: root stress and tip-load deflection against Euler-Bernoulli beam theory
first six natural frequencies from the modal analysis
equivalent stress at 20 m/s, against a 2.5E+08 Pa steel yield strength

hero.caption: Tip deflection of the blade under pressure, rotation and gravity

sections.heading: Three load cases
body: I modelled a steel blade in ANSYS Static Structural. Case A combined a 1190 Pa pressure load with rotation at 1.5708 rad/s and gravity, the closest of the three to real operation. Case B applied the pressure load alone, and Case C applied a 109 kN force at the tip.

Tip deflection came to 0.147 m for case A, 0.269 m for case B and 0.631 m for case C. In case A, maximum equivalent stress was 1.99E+08 Pa, against a steel yield strength of 2.5E+08 Pa, and sat at the transition from the hub to the blade.

figures.caption: Equivalent stress for the combined load case
Equivalent stress under the concentrated tip load

sections.heading: Checking against beam theory
body: Euler-Bernoulli beam theory gave a root stress of 1.74E+07 Pa and tip deflections of 0.651 m for the tip load and 0.392 m for the pressure load. The model agreed on root stress to within 3% and on tip-load deflection to 3.1%.

Pressure-load deflection differed by 37%. The analytical solution treats the load as a point force, while the model spreads it over the surface, so I took the numerical result as the more reliable one.

sections.heading: Mesh convergence
body: I refined the mesh from 1 m elements down to 0.15 m and tracked deflection and stress. Tip deflection converged. Peak equivalent stress kept rising as the mesh got finer, because the peak sits at the hub transition, where the loading and constraint create a stress singularity.

sections.heading: Natural frequencies
body: A modal analysis of the first six modes gave frequencies from 0.58 Hz to 7.5 Hz. Knowing where these natural frequencies sit helps avoid resonance in operation.

figures.caption: One of the six mode shapes from the modal analysis

sections.heading: Judging the design
body: At the 20 m/s upper design wind speed, the blade carries about 887 kN, which is equivalent to a 434.6 kN tip load. That produced an equivalent stress of 4.3E+08 Pa, well above the steel yield strength, so the blade is not safe at that speed.

Given the mesh result, I flagged that figure as needing a finer mesh or a physical test. I recommended a smoother change in geometry from the circular root to the blade, a fatigue analysis for the varying wind speed, and a material able to take 20 m/s.

evidence: The coursework report can be shared on request.

title: Battery Manufacturing Digital Twin and Life Cycle Assessment
summary: A digital twin of a battery cell-finishing station, checked against lab hardware, then extended into a facility layout and a life cycle assessment.

facts.label: of demand met by one arm (42,092 of 177,500 cells a year)
output from a dual-arm layout (84,184 cells a year)
energy under-prediction found by testing the twin against hardware

hero.caption: Dual-arm cell-finishing station in the digital twin

sections.heading: The problem
body: Two Quanser QArm robot arms sort 18650 battery cells by colour at a cell-finishing station. The questions were whether the station can keep up with production, and how far a simulation of it can be trusted.
A QLabs digital twin ran in parallel with the physical lab hardware, using OpenCV colour detection and inverse kinematics for the arm motion, written in Python.

sections.heading: Throughput
body: From the sorting cycle time and failure downtime, I estimated single-arm throughput at 42,092 cells per year against a demand of 177,500. That is 23.7% of the requirement, so the station is the bottleneck. A dual-arm layout doubles output to 84,184 cells per year.

figures.caption: Dual-arm configuration in operation

sections.heading: Testing the twin against hardware
body: The twin under-predicted the energy per sorting cycle by 93.6%: 46.7 J simulated against 128.83 J measured. Comparing current and PWM profiles traced the gap to friction and heating losses that the twin does not model.
Reporting that gap, and where it comes from, is what makes the throughput figure usable.

sections.heading: From station to factory
body: I extended the work into a facility layout using a relationship matrix, a bill of materials and a materials requirements plan across two cell chemistries, applying Industry 4.0 and continuous improvement principles.
An ISO 14040 life cycle assessment then compared LFP, sodium-ion and diesel and gasoline vehicle propulsion.

figures.caption: Facility layout with exclusion zones
Weighted LCA impacts: diesel, gasoline, LFP and sodium-ion

takeaway: A simulation is only as useful as its validation. Checking the twin against hardware showed where it was wrong and why, which mattered more than the throughput figure itself.
evidence: The full 27-page coursework report can be shared on request.

title: CTD Instrument for Coral Reef Monitoring
context: SESM3029 Engineering Design with Management, University of Southampton
role: Team of six. I designed the instrument main body, and worked on battery selection and the battery management circuit.
summary: A conductivity, temperature and depth instrument for coral reef monitoring, designed to integrate into an autonomous underwater vehicle, from housing to power system.

facts.label: lithium polymer pack, chosen from six chemistries
calculated mission runtime
battery protections: overcharge, deep discharge, short circuit, thermal

sections.heading: The brief
body: A National Oceanography Centre brief: a novel CTD (conductivity, temperature, depth) instrument for coral reef monitoring, designed to integrate into an autonomous underwater vehicle. I helped turn it into engineering requirements and clear design objectives.

sections.heading: Housing
body: I designed the instrument main body. Design concepts were compared on mechanical performance, material selection and manufacturing feasibility, and structural integrity and design margins were checked with hand calculations.

I ran CFD on candidate designs at 1 m/s and 50 m depth to compare their flow behaviour, looking for the lowest pressure change and so the least turbulent flow. Structural FEA under hydrostatic pressure at 30 m and 100 m depth justified the material choice.

figures.caption: CFD flow over a candidate housing design at 1 m/s
Structural FEA under hydrostatic pressure

sections.heading: Power
body: For the power system I compared six battery chemistries on energy density, power density, temperature range and cycle life, then sized a 7 Ah lithium polymer pack.
I designed the battery management circuit with overcharge, deep-discharge, short-circuit and thermal protection, and calculated a mission runtime of 8.2 hours.

figures.caption: Battery management circuit and PCB layout

takeaway: A design brief becomes clear once every choice is tied to a requirement and a number. Working from the deployment constraints to the battery size made each decision easy to defend.
evidence: The group report can be shared on request.

title: H2OME: Mars Settlement Siting
context: GirlsWhoML x PhysicsX Mars City Hackathon
role: Team of three. I built the household unit model and the sizing optimiser.
summary: A closed-loop household energy and water system for Mars, sized site by site, with a Gaussian process model to assess thousands of candidate locations.

facts.label: delivered per sol at 95% reliability, per site
solar-powered sites around 8 water-mining hubs
habitable latitude, extended by hydrogen from the hubs

hero.caption: Settlement layout: 80 sites around 8 water-mining hubs, self-sufficient and hub-supported scenarios (team output)

sections.heading: The brief
body: Plan a self-sufficient Mars settlement that closes the loop on energy, water and oxygen. Our team placed 80 solar-powered sites around 8 water-mining hubs.

sections.heading: The household unit
body: I designed the household unit, one closed loop replicated across every site. Solar power runs the home and charges a battery for the night. Shared ice excavation feeds an electrolyser that splits water into oxygen and hydrogen.
The hydrogen either backs up the home through dust storms via a fuel cell, or reacts with atmospheric CO2 in a Sabatier reactor to give exportable methane and water that returns to the loop.

sections.heading: The optimiser
body: I built the optimiser that sizes each site's solar array and battery to deliver 400 kWh per sol at 95% reliability, based on that site's own conditions rather than one fixed design.

sections.heading: The team result
body: My two teammates built a Gaussian process model around the physics simulation, so we could assess thousands of candidate sites. Together we found that pure solar works only up to about 55 degrees latitude, and that hydrogen piped in from the hubs extends habitation to 84 degrees.

takeaway: Sizing every site to its own conditions gave a better answer than copying one design 80 times, and a surrogate model made that search across thousands of sites possible in a hackathon. It was also where I learned to work with AI coding tools, Claude Code and Cursor.
evidence: The full code is public in the repository above. My work is the household unit model and the sizing optimiser.

title: Simulation Software QA and Automation at Siemens DISW
context: Software Engineering Intern, Simcenter FLOEFD QA team
role: QA engineer across two release cycles, owning the EDA Bridge and Component Explorer test areas.
summary: Quality assurance for a CAD-embedded CFD platform used for electronics thermal management, across two releases, plus automation that saved days per release.

facts.label: of engineering time saved per release cycle
major releases tested end to end (2412 and 2506)
CAD platforms covered by QA

sections.heading: The product
body: Simcenter FLOEFD is a CFD tool embedded in major CAD platforms, used heavily for electronics thermal management. I joined its QA team, testing internal builds before changes merged into the mainline, across five CAD tools.

sections.heading: Release 2412: owning a test area
body: After a handover from the outgoing interns, I specialised in EDA Bridge, which imports PCB and IC thermal properties into FLOEFD, and the Component Explorer, which lists component material and thermal data. This deepened my understanding of junction temperature, thermal resistance and power dissipation in simulation setup.

Late in the cycle I found a critical defect in how component data was displayed, which put simulation integrity at risk. I gave developers detailed reproduction steps, and it was fixed in a service pack after launch.

sections.heading: Release 2506: harder problems
body: I tested a fix for an integer overflow in the computation of very high-fidelity meshes. That meant designing test cases with extremely fine meshes, and monitoring solver stability, memory use and the non-zero count of the solver matrices to make sure the failure condition was actually reached.

I also tested a new version of EDA Bridge, including component swapping and a new project export workflow, checking data integrity between exported and original projects, and ran localisation testing across language packs.

sections.heading: Automation
body: I built Python, C++ and VBA automation tools, including machine learning libraries such as PyTorch, that saved seven days of engineering time per release cycle.

One example: a Python tool that audits CAD installations across the team’s network of machines, reading versions of NX, CATIA V5, Creo and Solid Edge from paths and registry entries. It handles coexisting NX builds and executables shared with Simcenter 3D. The QA team adopted it for system audits.

sections.heading: Working with the team
body: I worked in agile sprints with developers, product managers and QA engineers, writing bug reports developers could act on and designing test cases around customer workflows. Later in the year I helped onboard newer interns by explaining workflows and reviewing their test cases.
The code and internal tools are Siemens property, so they are not published here. I am happy to talk through the problems, approach and results in a conversation.

takeaway: Automation earns its place when it is tied to a measurable saving. Knowing the release process well enough to find what to automate came from doing the QA work first.
